title: Back To The Men Of The Trees
gist: Paywalled teaser: Charles Gave revives his framework that left/right politics is obsolete, replaced by a divide between localists ('men of the trees') and globalists ('men of the boats'), a typology drawn from Tahiti. The rest of the argument is behind the paywall.

themes.theme: Localists vs globalists replace left vs right

insights.claim: Charles Gave argues the traditional left-versus-right political distinction is obsolete and should be replaced by a split between localists ('men of the trees') and globalists ('men of the boats').
insights.speaker: Charles Gave
insights.so_what: A localist-vs-globalist lens can better predict policy on trade, migration and capital flows than party labels.
insights.quote: the old political distinction between the left and the right was obsolete
insights.locator: A few years ago, I proposed

insights.claim: Gavekal's Charles Gave is revisiting his earlier 'Trump And The Tree People' framework, implying he sees the localist-versus-globalist divide as newly relevant to current politics and markets in late 2026.
insights.speaker: Charles Gave
insights.so_what: Signals a renewed localist political tide; watch for policies favoring deglobalization, tariffs and domestic production.
insights.locator: Back To The Men Of The Trees

themes.theme: Tahitian origin of the tree/boat typology

insights.claim: Gave's localist/globalist typology comes from Tahiti, where society divides between those who stay beneath the familiar trees of their home island and those willing to cut down a tree, build a boat and sail elsewhere in search of something better.
insights.speaker: Charles Gave
insights.so_what: Frames the political cleavage as a preference for familiarity versus openness, the axis along which globalization policy is contested.
insights.quote: those willing to cut down a tree, build a boat and sail to another island in search of something better
